title: Issue-Spotting: Contract Formation (Offer, Acceptance, Consideration)
prompt: Read the fact pattern and write an IRAC analysis identifying the contract-formation issues. Facts: On Monday, Dana emails Rowan, a freelance illustrator: 'I'll pay you $4,000 to design a logo for my bakery. I need it by Friday. Let me know.' Rowan replies Tuesday morning: 'Sounds good — I can do it for $4,000, but I'll need $500 up front for supplies.' Dana does not respond. On Wednesday, before hearing anything further, Rowan starts sketching and buys $500 of software and materials. On Thursday, Dana emails: 'Actually, my cousin will do it for free — never mind.' Rowan demands $4,000, or at least the $500 spent. Analyze whether an enforceable contract was formed and what Rowan's best arguments and likely recovery are. Write a structured IRAC (or multi-issue IRAC) response.
blurb: A classic 1L formation fact pattern — spot the counteroffer, the lapse, and the reliance angle, and analyze it with disciplined IRAC.

rubric.label: Issue spotting
rubric.description: Identifies the discrete formation issues: whether Dana's email was an offer, whether Rowan's reply was an acceptance or a counteroffer (mirror-image rule), whether any contract exists to breach, and reliance/promissory-estoppel as a fallback. Flags the UCC-vs-common-law threshold (services, so common law).

rubric.label: Rule statement
rubric.description: States the governing rules accurately: offer as manifestation of present intent with definite terms; mirror-image rule and counteroffer as rejection; acceptance and the mailbox/lapse rules; consideration as bargained-for exchange; promissory estoppel elements (promise, foreseeable reliance, actual reliance, injustice).

rubric.label: Application to facts
rubric.description: Ties each rule to specific facts — the $500-up-front term as a material variation making Tuesday's reply a counteroffer, Dana's silence as non-acceptance, no meeting of the minds, then Rowan's Wednesday expenditures as the reliance hook.

rubric.label: Counterarguments
rubric.description: Argues both sides: Rowan's 'I can do it for $4,000' as arguable acceptance with a mere request for an accommodation vs. a true counteroffer; whether reliance was reasonable before any acceptance; Dana's revocation-before-acceptance defense.

rubric.label: Conclusion
rubric.description: Reaches a defensible bottom line on likely recovery (no expectation damages for a $4,000 contract; best shot is $500 reliance via promissory estoppel or restitution), acknowledging uncertainty.

rubric.label: IRAC structure & organization
rubric.description: Uses clear IRAC (or CRAC) organization, separates issues, headings or signposting, no fact-dump; each issue is self-contained.

rubric.label: Precision & legal writing
rubric.description: Uses terms of art correctly (offer, counteroffer, revocation, consideration, promissory estoppel), avoids conclusory leaps, hedges appropriately.

reference.scenario: Common-law services contract (logo design — not goods, so no UCC Article 2). The pivotal move is that Rowan's Tuesday reply adds a new material term ($500 up front), which under the mirror-image rule is a counteroffer and operates as a rejection of Dana's offer. Dana never accepts the counteroffer (silence is not acceptance here), so no bilateral contract forms. Dana is free to revoke/withdraw before acceptance. That kills expectation damages ($4,000). Rowan's realistic path is promissory estoppel or restitution for the $500, and even that is weak because Rowan spent the money in reliance on a deal that was never closed and on his own counteroffer. A strong answer spots all of this and argues both sides on whether the reply was acceptance-with-a-request vs. counteroffer.
model_points: Threshold: common law governs (services, not goods), so mirror-image rule applies rather than UCC 2-207.
Issue 1 — Offer: Dana's Monday email is likely a valid offer: present intent, definite terms (price $4,000, subject matter logo, deadline Friday), communicated to an identifiable offeree.

Issue 2 — Acceptance vs. counteroffer: Rowan's 'I can do it for $4,000, but I'll need $500 up front' adds a new term. Under the mirror-image rule a purported acceptance that varies terms is a counteroffer and a rejection. Argue the other side: courts sometimes treat a request for a non-material accommodation as acceptance plus a mere inquiry (see Restatement (Second) 61 — acceptance not made conditional on the new term).

Issue 3 — Formation outcome: If it is a counteroffer, Dana's silence is not acceptance, so no contract. Dana's Thursday email is an effective revocation/rejection of the counteroffer, made before any acceptance.
Issue 4 — Consideration: If a contract existed, consideration is present (bargained-for exchange: money for design). But consideration is moot if no offer was ever accepted.

Issue 5 — Reliance fallback: Promissory estoppel (Restatement 90) — a promise Dana should reasonably expect to induce reliance, actual reliance (the $500 spend), and injustice avoidable only by enforcement. Weakness: Rowan relied before acceptance and arguably on his own counteroffer; reasonableness of pre-contract reliance is contestable.
Issue 6 — Restitution/quantum meruit: Rowan conferred no benefit on Dana (Dana never received the logo), so unjust enrichment is a poor fit; this cuts against recovery.
Damages: No expectation ($4,000). Best realistic recovery is the $500 reliance interest, and even that is uncertain.
Conclusion: Most likely no enforceable $4,000 contract; Rowan's strongest — but still weak — claim is $500 in reliance damages under promissory estoppel.

probes.trigger: candidate concludes a contract was formed at $4,000 without addressing the added term
probes.question: Rowan's reply added a $500-up-front term. Under the mirror-image rule, is that an acceptance or a counteroffer — and what does that do to formation?

probes.trigger: candidate treats Dana's silence as acceptance of the counteroffer
probes.question: Is silence ever acceptance? What would Dana have had to do to accept the counteroffer, and did that happen here?
If no contract formed, on what theory could Rowan recover anything, and what would the measure of damages be?

probes.trigger: candidate ignores UCC vs common law
probes.question: Which body of law governs this deal, and why does that choice matter for how you treat the varied term?

probes.trigger: candidate is conclusory on promissory estoppel
probes.question: Walk me through each element of promissory estoppel on these facts — was Rowan's reliance reasonable given he had only sent a counteroffer?

red_flags: Conclusory analysis: states 'there was a valid offer and acceptance so a contract exists' without engaging the added term.
Misses the mirror-image rule / counteroffer entirely.
Treats silence as acceptance without discussing the exceptions.
Awards $4,000 expectation damages despite no formation.
Applies UCC 2-207 to a services contract (wrong body of law).
No counterarguments — argues only one side.
Fact-dump with no rule statement, or rule statement with no application.
Confuses consideration with the reliance/estoppel analysis.
follow_ups: Suppose the reply had said 'Great, I accept — and by the way it'd help to get $500 up front, but no worries either way.' Does your formation analysis change?
Assume instead this were a sale of goods. How would UCC 2-207 change the counteroffer analysis?
If Dana had emailed 'I promise to hold this offer open until Friday,' would that be enforceable? What doctrine controls firm offers?
How would your damages analysis differ between promissory estoppel and expectation damages?
reference.exemplar_answer: Issue 1 (Offer): Dana's Monday email is likely an offer — it manifests present intent to be bound, with definite terms (logo, $4,000, Friday deadline) directed at Rowan. Rule: an offer is a manifestation of willingness to enter a bargain, made so a reasonable offeree would understand assent will conclude it. Application: the specific price, subject, and deadline satisfy definiteness. Conclusion: valid offer. Issue 2 (Acceptance vs. counteroffer): This is the crux. Rule: under the common law mirror-image rule, an acceptance must match the offer exactly; a reply that adds or varies a material term is a counteroffer, which rejects the original offer. Application: Rowan's reply adds a $500-advance term Dana never proposed — payment timing is material — making it a counteroffer. Counterargument: under Restatement (Second) 61, an acceptance is not invalidated by a request for a change unless it is made conditional on that change; 'I can do it for $4,000, but I'll need $500 up front' could be read as acceptance plus a separate request. On balance, the demand ('I'll need') reads as a condition, so counteroffer is the better characterization. Conclusion: likely a counteroffer, so no contract yet. Issue 3 (Formation/revocation): Rule: silence is generally not acceptance; an offeror may revoke any time before acceptance. Application: Dana never responded to the counteroffer, and her Thursday email revoked before Rowan accepted anything. Conclusion: no bilateral contract; nothing to breach. Issue 4 (Reliance fallback): Rule: promissory estoppel enforces a promise that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce reliance, where the promisee actually and reasonably relies and injustice can be avoided only by enforcement. Application: Rowan spent $500, but did so on his own outstanding counteroffer before any acceptance, making reliance arguably unreasonable; restitution also fails because Dana received no benefit. Conclusion: Rowan's strongest claim is $500 in reliance damages, and it is weak; expectation damages of $4,000 are unavailable because no contract formed. Overall: most likely no enforceable contract; recovery, if any, is limited to the $500 reliance interest.

interviewer_notes: This is a written IRAC exercise; the candidate types the analysis. Score primarily on issue-spotting and IRAC discipline, not on reaching a 'right' answer. The single most important spot is that the $500-up-front term converts Rowan's reply into a counteroffer under the mirror-image rule — if the candidate misses this and blithely finds a $4,000 contract, press with the 'acceptance or counteroffer?' probe. Reward candidates who argue BOTH sides of the counteroffer characterization (Restatement 61 accommodation-request vs. conditional term). Push conclusory writers to state a rule before applying it, and to separate consideration (a formation element) from promissory estoppel (a reliance-based substitute). Reserve the last probe for damages: a candidate who awards $4,000 has not internalized that no contract formed. Strong (senior-leaning) answers proactively raise the UCC-vs-common-law threshold and note that restitution fails for lack of benefit conferred.
